24: Underwater images, during the acquisition process, are affected by light absorption and scattering effects, and generally suffer from colour imbalance, insufficient contrast and texture degradation, which severely constrain the effectiveness of advanced vision tasks such as underwater object detection. This thesis focuses on the two core tasks of underwater image super-resolution reconstruction and object detection, proposes two improved deep-learning-based methods, and validates them through systematic experiments on public datasets.
25: For underwater image super-resolution reconstruction, this thesis proposes the Frequency-Spatial Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN). The core of this network is the Spatial-Frequency Awareness Module (SFAM), which combines the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) with Swin Transformer-based spatial-domain encoding. Using a dual-branch structure, it adaptively enhances the frequency-domain amplitude component and phase component separately, then restores them to the spatial domain via the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT), achieving deep integration of global frequency-domain information and local spatial-domain features. In addition, this thesis introduces a texture-structure joint loss function, which applies targeted constraints to the image texture layer and structure layer separately, explicitly supervising the recovery of high-frequency details and geometric edges, thereby compensating for the limitations of conventional pixel-level losses. Experiments on the public USR-248 and UFO-120 datasets show that FSCIN achieves PSNR of 30.04 dB and 25.98 dB respectively at x2 magnification, attains leading overall performance across multiple magnification factors, and delivers efficient reconstruction with only 30.70 GFLOPs and 0.55 M parameters.
26: For underwater image object detection, this thesis addresses the problems of YOLOv8 in underwater scenes - a limited local receptive field and insufficient feature representation capability for small objects - by designing a fine-grained feature extraction module to replace the original C2f module. This module is built collaboratively from three sub-modules: the Channel-Spatial Adaptive Enhancement Module precisely focuses on object edges and texture details through a channel-spatial dual attention mechanism; the Mamba-based Global Perception Module introduces a visual state space model to model global spatial dependencies with linear complexity; and the Multi-Scale Cross-Attention Fusion Module adaptively integrates local and global features through asymmetric convolution and cross-scale attention interaction. Experiments on the URPC2021 underwater object detection dataset show that, compared with the original YOLOv8, the improved model raises mAP50 by 1.8 percentage points and raises the small-object detection metric APs by 1.1 percentage points.

153: With the rapid development of fields such as marine resource exploitation, marine environmental monitoring and underwater engineering inspection, underwater vision technology has gradually become an important means of acquiring marine information. With the release of the New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan, an explicit requirement was set for China to become the world's principal AI innovation centre by 2030, and this includes key technical fields such as deep learning and image processing. Against this backdrop, underwater vision technology has become a core means of acquiring marine information. Among these, the acquisition of high-quality underwater images is the prerequisite for achieving accurate object detection. By raising the resolution and level of detail of underwater images through super-resolution reconstruction technology, and then combining this with object detection methods, precise perception for biological identification, target localisation and resource surveying can be achieved in systems such as underwater robots, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), providing reliable technical support for underwater scientific research and engineering.
154: The underwater imaging environment is complex, and light propagation is simultaneously affected by absorption and scattering. The absorption effect causes light of different wavelengths to attenuate at different rates; among them, blue light attenuates relatively slowly, causing images to exhibit a blue-green colour cast. The scattering effect deflects light from its original path: forward scattering blurs edge details, while backward scattering reduces contrast and sharpness. As a result, underwater images generally suffer from low contrast, colour distortion, blurred details and noise interference, which makes it difficult for traditional vision algorithms to accurately extract target features and limits the performance of detection systems, as shown in Figure 1.1. To cope with the complex interference of the underwater imaging environment, many scholars have taken a hardware approach and designed high-precision, high-speed cameras to improve image acquisition quality. Although such equipment reduces noise to a certain extent and mitigates the influence of the water body on imaging, the acquired images still lack fine detail and texture information and struggle to meet the requirements of subsequent object detection or analysis tasks; at the same time they are expensive, which is unfavourable for large-scale application. By contrast, underwater image super-resolution reconstruction technology can, without changing the original imaging equipment, restore details and textures lost in low-resolution images. This not only significantly improves image quality but also provides richer feature information for object detection, achieving effective coupling between image enhancement and target recognition, and thereby improving the accuracy and stability of underwater target localisation and recognition. As shown in Figure 1.2, processed underwater images can substantially increase the number of matched feature points.

160: In summary, this thesis proposes a complete underwater visual perception framework whose main thread is "original underwater image -> super-resolution sharpening -> high-quality clear image -> object detection -> detection result". This framework organically links the two modules of image quality improvement and object detection: first, a deep-learning-based super-resolution reconstruction method is used to enhance the originally degraded image, restoring its texture details, improving colour imbalance and raising contrast; then, with the high-quality clear image as input, an improved object detection model performs precise recognition and localisation of underwater targets. Experimental research shows that performing object detection after enhancement processing of underwater images can effectively improve the model's detection accuracy, thereby improving overall detection performance. Therefore, researching deep-learning-based underwater image super-resolution reconstruction and object detection methods has important theoretical significance and application value for improving the performance of underwater vision systems.

360: The underwater imaging environment is complex: during propagation, light is simultaneously affected by both absorption and scattering effects, and the degree of attenuation differs markedly for light of different wavelengths. This characteristic causes the underwater images acquired to generally exhibit visual defects such as colour imbalance, low contrast and texture degradation. These degradation phenomena not only affect human intuitive interpretation but also severely constrain the effectiveness of advanced applications such as underwater object detection, path planning and structural inspection. Super-resolution (SR) reconstruction technology, by inferring high-resolution output from low-resolution input, can effectively restore degraded structural and textural components in the image, and is currently an important technical means of improving image quality in underwater vision systems. Thanks to the wide-ranging breakthroughs of deep learning in image restoration, underwater image SR methods based on convolutional neural networks and Transformer architectures have successively emerged [18]. Such methods generally reconstruct high-frequency texture through multi-level spatial feature extraction and cascaded modules, and have achieved good reconstruction results on public datasets. However, the vast majority of the above methods perform feature modelling only within the spatial domain, and their exploitation of the global structural information and periodic patterns contained in the frequency domain remains very limited [32]; when faced with the complex and diverse degradation phenomena of underwater scenes, they struggle to stably capture global contextual cues and high-frequency detail. At the same time, existing methods mostly rely on pixel-level L1 loss or generic perceptual loss in their loss function design [7], and these loss functions have insufficient constraining power over image structural contours and fine textures. According to texture-structure decomposition theory, an image can be represented as the superposition of a structure layer and a texture layer; decoupling the two components and applying supervision to each separately can provide more targeted optimisation guidance during reconstruction [29]. Inspired by this, this chapter introduces a texture-structure joint loss, applying constraints respectively to high-frequency texture detail and low-frequency structural edges, so that the network can likewise recover perceptually realistic and geometrically accurate reconstruction results under complex underwater degradation conditions.
361: Addressing the limitations of existing methods, this chapter proposes a new Frequency-Spatial Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN), which achieves enhanced reconstruction of underwater image super-resolution by fusing frequency and spatial priors. FSCIN integrates the Spatial Frequency Awareness Module (SFAM), which performs joint modelling of the frequency domain and the spatial domain through the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Swin Transformer-based spatial encoding. SFAM aligns amplitude and phase information through dual-branch processing, thereby effectively capturing and enhancing the high-frequency components and global contextual information of the image. In addition, to maintain perceptual fidelity, this chapter also introduces a texture-structure joint constraint loss, which decomposes the reconstructed image into a texture layer and a structure layer and applies targeted supervision to each layer. This loss effectively constrains FSCIN to preserve the integrity of structural boundaries while reconstructing fine-grained visual detail. Extensive experimental results show that FSCIN demonstrates superior performance in reconstructing underwater images with good visual quality and accurate structure.

489: Addressing the underwater image super-resolution reconstruction task, this chapter has proposed the Frequency-Spatial Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN) to solve the problems of insufficient exploitation of frequency-domain information and the limited constraining power of loss functions. The network constructs a three-stage processing framework comprising low-level feature extraction, frequency-spatial collaborative feature enhancement and high-resolution image reconstruction; the function of each stage is clear and the coupling is reasonable, providing a good basis for the flexible replacement and extension of subsequent modules. The core spatial-frequency awareness module (SFAM) maps features into the frequency domain through the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), models the amplitude spectrum and phase spectrum separately using a dual-branch Swin Transformer attention structure, and then restores them to the spatial domain through the inverse Fourier transform (IFFT), achieving deep fusion of frequency-domain global perception and spatial-domain local modelling. The joint loss function, which applies supervision separately to the texture layer and the structure layer, effectively improves the reconstruction accuracy of high-frequency detail and geometric edges through the coordinated action of gradient-domain texture constraints and structure-extractor constraints. Experimental results show that FSCIN achieves optimal or highly competitive quantitative metrics at multiple magnification factors on the two public benchmark datasets USR-248 and UFO-120, while also demonstrating clearer texture restoration capability and higher structural fidelity in visual quality, providing a high-quality image pre-processing basis for the subsequent underwater object detection task. 493: Underwater object detection is one of the core tasks of underwater visual perception systems, and has important application value in fields such as marine biological monitoring, autonomous navigation of underwater robots and marine resource exploration. However, the underwater imaging environment is complex: as light propagates through water it is jointly affected by multiple factors such as scattering, absorption and refraction, causing underwater images generally to suffer from degradation phenomena such as low contrast, colour shift and blurred edges. These visual defects severely constrain the ability of object detection algorithms to extract effective features.
494: From the perspective of this thesis's overall "enhancement-detection" framework, the FSCIN super-resolution reconstruction network proposed in Chapter 3 has already systematically improved image quality with respect to the above degradation problems: through frequency-spatial collaborative modelling it reconstructs originally low-quality underwater images into high-quality images with clearer texture, more accurate colour and more complete edge information, achieving an optimal PSNR of 30.04dB at x2 magnification on the USR-248 dataset and a reconstruction accuracy of 24.03dB at x8 magnification with only 2.45GFLOPs, verifying the effectiveness and efficiency of the front-end enhancement module. The work of this chapter takes the sharpened images output by Chapter 3 as direct input, and builds an accurate underwater object detection model on the basis of these higher-quality images, realising the second stage of the complete processing chain "original image -> super-resolution sharpening -> clear image -> object detection -> detection result". Through this cascaded design, the object detection model can extract more effective target features from images with richer detail and higher contrast, thereby significantly improving the detection recall rate and localisation accuracy for tiny underwater targets. At present, one-stage detection methods represented by YOLOv8 still face the following main limitations when applied directly to underwater scenes [39][43]: first, YOLOv8 performs feature extraction with convolutional neural networks at its core, and being limited by the local receptive field it struggles to model long-range dependency relationships in the image, with somewhat deficient capability for capturing global contextual information; second, the original C2f module has insufficient fine-grained feature representation capability for small targets, and detection accuracy for tiny targets (such as sea urchins and scallops) under low-visibility underwater conditions is limited; third, although PAN-FPN-type structures can enhance multi-scale information fusion [38], in complex underwater scenes the appearance differences, occlusion and background interference of targets at different scales still weaken the model's adaptive fusion capability, making it difficult to simultaneously accommodate the detection requirements of targets at different scales.

501: The YOLO (You Only Look Once) family of algorithms is the representative approach in the current field of one-stage object detection. By modelling the detection task as a direct regression problem, it predicts target categories and bounding-box coordinates simultaneously within a single forward inference pass, achieving a good balance between detection speed and accuracy. YOLOv8 is a more recent version in this series, with a number of systematic improvements in network structure and training strategy.
502: In terms of the backbone network, YOLOv8 adopts a newly designed C2f module to replace the C3 module of the previous generation. The C2f module splits the input feature map into two branches - one passed through directly, the other undergoing deep feature extraction through multiple Bottleneck blocks - and finally concatenates and fuses all intermediate outputs, improving gradient flow while maintaining computational efficiency. In terms of feature fusion, YOLOv8 inherits the PAN-FPN structure, achieving bidirectional fusion of multi-scale features through a top-down semantic path and a bottom-up detail path, enhancing detection capability for targets at different scales. In terms of the detection head, YOLOv8 adopts a decoupled head design, processing the classification branch and the regression branch separately, reducing mutual interference between the two tasks and improving detection accuracy.

It is therefore necessary to make targeted improvements to YOLOv8 for the image characteristics of underwater scenes, in order to improve its detection robustness in complex underwater environments.
